# FIPS crypto module audit of serving-stack images

## Description

An Investigation that resolves which images in the model serving stack link non-validated cryptographic libraries, and which of those usages sit in the request path. The strategy asserts that KServe components and the serving data plane link non-validated crypto in several images, but does not enumerate them. The outcome determines the exact remediation scope for the serving images, the denylist for CI enforcement, and produces the module inventory required by the compliance evidence package.

## Scope

- Enumerate every container image in the serving stack: KServe components and the Platform Operator image.
- For each image, inventory the linked cryptographic libraries and modules and their provenance (base image, language runtime, direct dependency).
- Classify each module as FIPS-validated (listed on the applicable validated-modules registry) or non-validated.
- Identify which non-validated usages are in the request path versus incidental (not exercised when serving inference requests).
- Produce a remediation list: per image, each non-validated request-path usage with a recommended validated replacement, or an explicit flag that no validated replacement exists.
- Deliverable: a module inventory and remediation list that the image remediation work, the CI regression gate, and the compliance evidence package can all consume without re-deriving it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every serving-stack image (KServe components and the Platform Operator image) has a complete crypto module inventory entry with a validated/non-validated classification — no image left without a disposition.
- Each non-validated usage is marked as request-path or incidental, with the linkage path recorded.
- Each remediation item names the image, the library, and either a recommended validated replacement or an explicit "no validated replacement available" flag.
- The inventory is reproducible: the method used to derive it is documented so a re-run after remediation can confirm the result.

## HLR Traceability

- Enables HLR-1 (P0): determines the remediation scope for running the serving stack on validated crypto modules.
- Provides the module inventory input for HLR-2 (P0) and the denylist source for HLR-3 (P1).

# Run KServe serving images on validated crypto modules

## Description

Remediate the KServe serving images so that no non-validated cryptographic library is linked in the request path, and the images run correctly on FIPS-enabled OpenShift clusters. This delivers the KServe half of the requirement that all serving-stack images operate on validated crypto modules.

## Scope

- For each KServe image flagged by the crypto module audit, replace or rebuild so request-path crypto uses validated modules (for example via FIPS-validated base images or validated provider modules).
- Changes are confined to build recipes, base images, and dependency pins in the KServe midstream repos; serving behavior is unchanged.
- Verify end-to-end inference on a FIPS-enabled OpenShift cluster (serverless and raw deployment modes where applicable).
- Produce build attestations for each remediated image for use in the compliance evidence package.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Re-running the crypto module audit on the remediated KServe images shows no non-validated crypto library linked in the request path.
- A sample model served via InferenceService answers inference requests end-to-end on a FIPS-enabled OpenShift cluster.
- Build attestations for each remediated KServe image are produced and available to the compliance evidence package.
- Rollback: the previous image versions remain deployable, so a remediated image that fails in production can be replaced (this work replaces existing image builds).

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-1 (P0): all serving-stack images run correctly on FIPS-enabled clusters using validated crypto modules — KServe portion.

# CI gating check for FIPS crypto regressions in serving-stack builds

## Description

A gating CI check that fails any serving-stack build which reintroduces non-validated cryptographic library usage, so FIPS compliance cannot silently regress once the images are remediated.

## Scope

- Implement a check that inspects built serving-stack images (or their dependency trees) for non-validated crypto libraries, using the module inventory and validation-registry statuses established by the crypto module audit as its reference data.
- Wire the check as a required, gating step in the CI pipelines for all serving-stack builds, covering both the KServe repos and the Platform Operator repo.
- Ensure failure output identifies the offending library and image so the regression is actionable.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The check runs on every serving-stack build pipeline (KServe and Platform Operator) and is gating: a failure blocks the build or merge.
- A build that deliberately introduces a non-validated crypto library fails the check (verified by a negative test).
- A build using only validated crypto modules passes the check.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-3 (P1): CI enforces FIPS regressions — a gating check fails any serving-stack build that reintroduces non-validated crypto usage.

# Assemble and submit the FIPS compliance evidence package

## Description

Assemble the compliance evidence package — module inventory, build attestations, and test results — for the model serving stack, drive it through the mandatory security review board sign-offs at the defined milestones, and submit it to the external accredited certification lab. This is the deliverable that converts engineering work into a certification submission.

## Scope

- Compile the module inventory from the crypto module audit, build attestations from the remediated serving-stack images, and FIPS-enabled cluster test results from the remediation verification.
- Structure the package according to the certification lab's evidence requirements.
- Coordinate the security review board sign-offs at the defined milestones.
- Submit the package to the external accredited certification lab and drive its triage to acceptance of the submission.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The evidence package contains the module inventory, build attestations for every serving-stack image, and FIPS-enabled cluster test results.
- The package passes the internal security review board sign-offs at the defined milestones.
- The package is submitted to the external accredited certification lab and triaged (accepted as a complete submission).

## Risks / Notes

- Lab turnaround is historically six to nine months and review-board cadence is externally controlled; neither can be compressed by engineering effort. These are schedule risks on this epic, not engineering completion criteria — the epic's completion point is the submitted-and-triaged package.

## HLR Traceability

- HLR-2 (P0): a compliance evidence package (module inventory, build attestations, test results) is assembled and submitted through the security review board to the external certification lab.

Then evaluate each independently:\n82\t\n83\t**Decision rule: Does the answer change which downstream epics exist or what they do?**\n84\t\n85\t- **YES** → Investigation epic. Determine which downstream epics depend on the outcome. Add as DAG edges. For bounded outcomes (≤3 possibilities): output conditional decomposition branches.\n86\t- **NO** → Acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic. Implementation proceeds the same way regardless; failure = fix-and-retry.\n87\t\n88\tMultiple independent unknowns can produce multiple Investigation epics, even for the same component and team. The component/team boundary rule applies to Implementations (bundling work for a team), not Investigations (resolving a specific unknown). However, if two qualifying unknowns would be resolved by the same experiment producing the same deliverable, combine them into one Investigation — don't split for the sake of splitting.\n89\t\n90\t## Step 4: Map HLRs to Epics\n91\t\n92\t**Precondition:** This step only runs for strategies that were NOT triaged in Step 0. If Step 0 produced a below-threshold or docs-only result, the strategy is already a single epic — do not apply priority-split logic.\n93\t\n94\t- Each P0/P1/P2 requirement must map to one or more epics\n95\t- Every HLR must be covered — no orphaned requirements\n96\t- Priority inheritance: prerequisite epic inherits the highest priority of all HLRs it transitively enables\n97\t- An epic blocking all P0 work is implicitly P0\n98\t- Priority split: when an epic maps to HLRs at multiple priority levels, check whether the lower-priority HLRs represent distinct, deferrable features. A feature is \"distinct and deferrable\" only when it could ship as its own epic with independent user value AND does not share data structures, UI surfaces, or API endpoints with the P0 work. If yes, split them into separate epics by priority so each can be planned independently. If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n111\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n112\t\n113\t### Investigation Edges\n114\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n115\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n116\t\n117\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n118\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n119\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.\n120\t7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)\n121\t8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)\n122\t9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)\n123\t10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` (\"the code needs a build pipeline first\") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation.\n124\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n125\t\n126\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n127\t12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)\n128\t13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel.\n129\t14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel\n130\t15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n131\t\n132\t### External Dependency Edges\n133\t16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)\n134\t17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)\n135\t18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)\n136\t\n137\t### Epic Generation Rules\n138\t19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation\n139\t20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).\n140\t21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n141\t22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation\n142\t\n143\t### Acceptance Criteria Rules\n144\t23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Strategy cites specific architecture context files/APIs | Unsubstantiated architecture claims |\n195\t\n196\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n197\t\n198\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n199\t\n200\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n201\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n202\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n203\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n204\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n205\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n206\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n207\t\n208\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n209\t\n210\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n211\t\n212\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n213\t\n214\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n215\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n216\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n217\t\n218\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n219\t\n220\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n221\t\n222\t| Situation | Handling |\n223\t|-----------|---------|\n224\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n225\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n226\t\n227\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n228\t\n229\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n230\t\n231\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n232\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n233\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n234\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n235\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n236\t\n237\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable. External schedule constraints are not ACs: turnaround you do not control (accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC.\n238\t\n239\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n240\t\n241\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n242\t\n243\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n244\t\n245\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n246\t\n247\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n248\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n249\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n250\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n251\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n252\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n253\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n254\t\n255\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n256\t\n257\t```bash\n258\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n259\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n260\t```\n261\t\n262\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n263\t\n264\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n265\t\n266\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n267\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n268\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n269\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n270\tfor the implementing team.\n271\t\n272\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n273\t\n274\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n275\t\n276\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n277\t\n278\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n279\t   - **Title** (one line)\n280\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n281\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n282\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n283\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n284\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n285\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n286\t\n287\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n288\t\n289\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n290\t\n291\t```bash\n292\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n293\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n294\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n295\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n296\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n297\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n298\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n299\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n302\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n303\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n304\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n305\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n306\t```\n307\t\n308\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n309\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n310\t\n311\t```bash\n312\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n313\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n314\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n315\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n316\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n317\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n318\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n319\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n320\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n321\t```\n322\t\n323\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n324\t\n325\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n326\t\n327\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n328\t\n329\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n330\t```\n331\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n332\t```\n333\t\n334\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.\n335\t\n336\tThen run the contract validator until it passes:\n337\t\n338\t```bash\n339\tpython3 skills/epic-decompose/scripts/validate_decomposition.py {ID}\n340\t```\n341\t\n342\tIt deterministically checks what downstream consumers enforce and an LLM step can silently get wrong: epic body sections (Description / Scope / Acceptance Criteria / HLR Traceability), `component` values verbatim in `.context/rhai-components.txt`, Rule 11 (docs-authoring blocked by every Implementation epic), and priority inheritance (an epic blocking P0 work is itself P0). It prints one `VIOLATION:` line per problem and exits non-zero. Fix every violation by editing the epic files (never edit the script), re-run, and proceed only once it prints `OK`.\n343\t\n344\tThen, as your **final action** — after every epic file is written, any divergence is fixed, and the validator prints `OK` — mark the decomposition complete:\n345\t\n346\t```\n347\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n348\t```\n349\t\n350\tThe pipeline uses this field to detect that you have finished. Until it is set, the review agent is not launched.
